sections.title: 1 · Power Electronics in Sixty Seconds
ps: Power = Voltage × Current (P = V·I). Moving the same power at higher voltage means lower current — and since wiring losses grow with the square of current (I²R), doubling voltage cuts copper losses to a quarter and lets you use much thinner cable. This one equation explains most of what Megmeet builds.
The grid runs on AC (alternating current — easy to change voltage with transformers); every chip, battery, and LED runs on DC (direct current). Something must always convert between them.

The four conversion machines: a RECTIFIER turns AC into DC; an INVERTER turns DC into AC; a DC-DC CONVERTER changes one DC voltage to another; a TRANSFORMER changes AC voltage. Every Megmeet product is some stack of these four.

Modern converters don't use big iron transformers — they chop current with semiconductor switches at tens or hundreds of kilohertz, which shrinks the magnetics dramatically. New wide-bandgap semiconductors (silicon carbide 'SiC' and gallium nitride 'GaN') switch faster with less loss, which is why converters keep getting smaller and more efficient.

Efficiency compounds and losses become heat: a chain of five 97%-efficient stages delivers only ~86% of the power. At megawatt scale, every 1% lost is ~10 kW of heat per MW that you must also pay to cool. This is why the industry fights over single percentage points.

sections.title: 2 · How a Data Center Is Powered Today (the chain being disrupted)
ps: The legacy chain: grid MEDIUM VOLTAGE (10–35 kV AC) → step-down transformer → 400/480 V AC 'low voltage' → UPS (uninterruptible power supply: converts AC→DC to charge batteries, then DC→AC back out, so a grid blip never reaches the servers) → PDU (power distribution unit) → rack → each server's PSU (power supply unit, AC→12/48 V DC) → tiny voltage regulators on the board (→ ~1 V at hundreds of amps for the chips).
Each stage exists for a reason (safety, backup, distribution) — but the power gets converted five or more times, each conversion wasting a little and adding equipment that takes floor space.

This architecture was fine when a rack drew 5–15 kW. AI racks (dense GPU clusters) draw 100 kW+ today and are headed for 1 MW per rack. At 415 V AC, feeding 1 MW takes roughly 1,400 amps — meaning enormous copper busbars, breakers, and I²R losses. The old chain physically stops making sense.

Key vocabulary: PUE (power usage effectiveness) = total facility power ÷ power that actually reaches computing. PUE 1.5 means 50% overhead (conversion losses + cooling); PUE 1.1 means only 10%. Lower PUE = millions saved per site per year.

sections.title: 3 · The 800 VDC Shift — Each Megmeet Product's Slot in the New Chain
ps: The industry's fix (led by NVIDIA's rack architectures): convert to DC once, early, at a high voltage — 800 V DC — and distribute that to the racks. Fewer conversion stages, ~5% better end-to-end efficiency, and ~45% less copper. Megmeet builds a product for every stage of this new chain.

SOLID-STATE TRANSFORMER (SST) — the endgame product. A power-electronics 'smart transformer' that takes medium-voltage AC straight from the grid and outputs 800 V DC in one box (>98.5% efficient, megawatt-scale), replacing the transformer + rectifier layers and part of the UPS role. This is what enables PUE below 1.1.

800 V HVDC SIDECAR — the bridge product shipping now. An external cabinet standing next to the rack that converts a building's EXISTING 480/380 V AC into 800 V DC, delivering >1 MW to a single rack — so operators get the new architecture's benefits without rebuilding the whole facility. Designed for NVIDIA's Kyber-class dense racks.

POWER SHELVES — slide-in conversion trays inside the rack (33 kW air-cooled; 110 kW liquid-cooled for GB300/Vera Rubin-class racks) that feed the rack's DC busbar. Built 'N+1': one more module than needed, so any single module can fail or be hot-swapped while the rack keeps running.

BBU & SUPERCAPACITOR SHELVES — backup moved into the rack. The BBU (battery backup unit, 16.5 kW) rides through outages of seconds to minutes; the supercapacitor shelf (15 kW) absorbs millisecond spikes and dips — critical because GPU clusters swing their power draw violently between training steps. Together they replace much of the central UPS.

CRPS / M-CRPS SERVER PSUs — the standardized power modules inside servers (an industry form factor, so any vendor's unit fits any compliant server). Megmeet's run 800 W to 5.5 kW at >100 W per cubic inch — about double traditional density — with efficiency grades named like medals (80 PLUS Titanium = 96%; Ruby is the new top tier).
POWER BRICK — the last step: a converter mounted near the GPU that takes 54 V or 800 V down to the ~1 V the silicon actually drinks.

Why the 110 kW shelf is LIQUID-cooled: at that density air physically can't carry the heat away fast enough; cold plates with ~45°C 'warm' liquid do — and warm liquid is cheap to re-cool (or reuse) compared to chilled air.

Where energy storage fits: an AI campus's load swings stress the grid, so battery storage (BESS) buffers between grid and data center — Megmeet also makes storage power conversion and the monitoring/EMS layer for this 'compute-power coordination.'

sections.title: 4 · The Same Physics Everywhere Else in Their Portfolio
ps: VARIABLE-FREQUENCY DRIVES (industrial automation — MV800/MV520 series): rectify grid AC, then re-synthesize AC at any frequency to control a motor's speed. Electric motors consume roughly 45% of the world's electricity, and most run at full speed behind a throttle — matching speed to actual load saves 20–50%. Servo drives (M5) are the precision version for robotics; PLCs (MU series) are the factory's control brain.

EV COMPONENTS (Geely, BAIC, Leapmotor…): a car is a rolling power-electronics chain — the OBC (onboard charger) rectifies wall AC into battery DC; the DC-DC converter steps the 400/800 V pack down to 12 V for accessories; the motor controller is an inverter turning battery DC into 3-phase AC that spins the traction motor. Megmeet shipped 1M+ combined OBC+DC-DC units in 2025.

APPLIANCE INVERTER CONTROLS (their biggest business — Xiaomi, Haier, Hisense): an 'inverter' air conditioner or heat pump uses a variable-speed drive on its compressor instead of crude on-off cycling — the same VFD idea shrunk onto an appliance board. Quieter, longer-lived, and far more efficient; heat pumps are this concept applied to whole-home heating.

WELDING INVERTERS (Artsen/Dex series): chop DC at 64–180 kHz through a small transformer to get a precisely controllable arc — replacing the old transformer welders that weighed ten times as much. Digital control means spatter reduction, repeatable robot welding (1,800-unit repeat order from a steel-structure builder), and cloud-connected weld quality (SMARC).
PRECISION CONNECTION: the specialized conductors — shaped magnet wire, flat flexible cable (FFC/FPC) — that wind the magnetics and link the battery packs everything above depends on.

The unifying thread: one competence — fast semiconductor switching plus digital control — applied to appliances, factories, cars, welders, and now AI data centers. That's why one company plausibly plays in all six markets.

sections.title: 5 · Industry Map — Who Buys, Who Competes, Why It Matters
ps: Who defines the market: NVIDIA publishes the rack architectures (GB300, Vera Rubin, Kyber; MGX standard) and blesses a power ecosystem. Megmeet is a member of NVIDIA's 800 V HVDC alliance and the only mainland-China power supplier NVIDIA named for GB200 NVL72 racks. Hyperscalers (the giant cloud/AI builders) are the ultimate buyers.

Who it competes with: server power is ~74% Taiwanese — Delta Electronics alone ~41%, plus Lite-On, AcBel, Chicony, Advanced Energy. Incumbents win stable architectures; challengers win architecture TRANSITIONS — which is exactly why Megmeet moved first on the 800 VDC sidecar/SST chain rather than fighting Delta head-on in yesterday's PSU sockets.

The economics of a percentage point: a 100 MW AI campus at 8.8 ¢/kWh pays ~$77M/year for power — so a 5% end-to-end efficiency gain is worth millions per site per year before even counting the smaller cooling plant and reclaimed floor space.

The timeline: 33 kW/110 kW shelves and sidecars are shipping into today's racks; full 800 VDC facilities with 1 MW racks are projected from ~2027 (the Rubin/Kyber era). The bet is on owning the stages of that chain before it becomes the standard.

Adjacent pull-through: the same high-voltage conversion platform feeds energy storage (PCS), EV fast charging (40 kW charging modules launched Jul 2026), and telecom power — one R&D investment amortized across several end markets.

flashcards.q: Why does the industry keep pushing distribution voltage UP (415 V AC → 800 V DC)?
flashcards.a: P = V·I — at higher voltage the same power needs less current, and wiring losses scale with current squared (I²R). Doubling voltage cuts copper losses to a quarter and allows much thinner conductors. At 415 V AC, a 1 MW rack needs ~1,400 A of copper; at 800 V DC it's manageable.

flashcards.q: Rectifier vs inverter vs DC-DC converter — what does each do?
flashcards.a: Rectifier: AC → DC. Inverter: DC → AC. DC-DC converter: one DC voltage → another. (A transformer changes AC voltage.) Every power-electronics product is a stack of these four blocks.

flashcards.q: What does a solid-state transformer (SST) do, and what does it replace?
flashcards.a: It takes medium-voltage AC directly from the grid and outputs 800 V DC in one power-electronics box at >98.5% efficiency — replacing the conventional step-down transformer + rectifier stages and part of the UPS role. It's the product that enables PUE below 1.1.

flashcards.q: What is the 800 V HVDC 'sidecar' and why is it called a bridge product?
flashcards.a: An external cabinet beside the rack that converts a building's EXISTING 480/380 V AC to 800 V DC, delivering >1 MW to one rack. It gives operators the new DC architecture's benefits (less copper, better efficiency) without rebuilding the facility — bridging until full 800 VDC facilities arrive (~2027).

flashcards.q: What is a power shelf, and what does 'N+1' mean?
flashcards.a: A slide-in conversion tray in the rack that feeds the rack's DC busbar (Megmeet: 33 kW air-cooled, 110 kW liquid-cooled). N+1 means one more module than the load requires, so any single module can fail or be hot-swapped without the rack going down.

flashcards.q: Why do AI racks need BOTH battery (BBU) and supercapacitor shelves?
flashcards.a: They cover different timescales: batteries ride through outages lasting seconds to minutes; supercapacitors absorb millisecond spikes and sags. GPU clusters swing power draw violently between compute steps, so both layers replace much of the old central UPS — moved right into the rack.

flashcards.q: What is a CRPS/M-CRPS power supply, and why do Titanium/Ruby efficiency grades matter?
flashcards.a: An industry-standard form factor for server PSUs (any compliant vendor's module fits). Grades are efficiency medals — 80 PLUS Titanium ≈ 96%, Ruby is the newer top tier. At data-center scale, each percentage point of PSU efficiency is real money in both electricity and the cooling to remove the waste heat.

flashcards.q: What is PUE and what does PUE < 1.1 mean?
flashcards.a: Power Usage Effectiveness = total facility power ÷ power delivered to computing. PUE 1.5 = 50% overhead lost to conversions and cooling; PUE 1.1 = only 10% overhead — the target the 800 VDC + SST architecture is designed to hit.

flashcards.q: Why is the 110 kW power shelf liquid-cooled?
flashcards.a: At that power density, air physically can't carry heat away fast enough. Cold plates with ~45°C 'warm' liquid can — and warm liquid is far cheaper to re-cool than chilled air, which also helps facility PUE.

flashcards.q: What does a variable-frequency drive (VFD) do, and why does it save so much energy?
flashcards.a: It rectifies grid AC to DC, then re-synthesizes AC at any frequency to control motor speed. Motors eat ~45% of world electricity and mostly run full-speed behind throttles — matching speed to load saves 20–50%. An 'inverter' air conditioner is the same idea on a compressor.

flashcards.q: In an EV, what do the OBC, DC-DC converter, and motor controller each do?
flashcards.a: OBC (onboard charger): wall AC → battery DC. DC-DC: 400/800 V pack → 12 V for accessories. Motor controller: an inverter turning battery DC into 3-phase AC to spin the traction motor. A modern EV is a rolling power-electronics chain.

flashcards.q: Why did welding machines move to high-frequency inverters?
flashcards.a: Chopping DC at 64–180 kHz lets a small transformer do what a huge iron one did, and digital control of the arc gives precise, repeatable welds (less spatter, robot-ready) — which is why fabricators order robotic welding power sources by the thousand.

flashcards.q: What are SiC and GaN, and why do they matter?
flashcards.a: Wide-bandgap semiconductors (silicon carbide, gallium nitride) that switch faster with lower losses than silicon. Faster switching shrinks the magnetics, so converters get smaller, cooler, and more efficient — they're the enabling ingredient of the whole 800 VDC/high-density power wave.

flashcards.q: Where does battery energy storage (BESS) fit in AI data-center power?
flashcards.a: Between the grid and the campus: AI training loads swing hard and fast, which stresses the grid, so storage buffers those swings ('compute-power coordination'). The same high-voltage conversion technology used in the data center also builds the storage PCS and EV fast chargers.

flashcards.q: Why does an architecture transition (AC → 800 VDC) create an opening for a challenger against a ~41%-share incumbent like Delta?
flashcards.a: Incumbents' advantages — installed base, qualified designs, scale — are tied to the OLD architecture. When the architecture changes, every socket is re-competed, and the vendor who co-designed the new chain earliest (SST, sidecar, shelves) starts even or ahead.
